A_target.statement:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a [[Definition:Triangle (Geometry)|triangle]] and let $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ be [[Definition:Cevian|cevians]] meeting at an interior point $P$, with $D$, $E$, $F$ on $BC$, $CA$, $AB$.
Then:
:$\dfrac {BD} {DC} \cdot \dfrac {CE} {EA} \cdot \dfrac {AF} {FB} = 1$

B_source.statement:
For a [[Definition:Transversal (Geometry)|transversal]] meeting $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$, write each ratio $\dfrac {BD} {DC}$ etc. as a ratio of areas of triangles with a common height.
Multiplying the three ratios, the areas cancel, which gives [[Menelaus's Theorem]].

substitutions.triangles with apex on the transversal: triangles with apex at the common point P

derived.cancelling areas: the product of the three ratios equals 1

object_map.reformulation: Reuse the area-ratio plan of Menelaus, but compare areas of the three triangles cut out by P.

validity_conditions: Triangles with the same apex and bases on one line have areas proportional to the bases.
For an interior point P all areas are positive, so unsigned ratios suffice.
proof_plan:
Triangles $ABD$ and $ADC$ have the same height from $A$, so $\dfrac {BD} {DC} = \dfrac {\sqbrk {ABD} } {\sqbrk {ADC} }$.
Likewise $\dfrac {BD} {DC} = \dfrac {\sqbrk {PBD} } {\sqbrk {PDC} }$.

If $\dfrac a b = \dfrac c d = k$ then $\dfrac {a - c} {b - d} = k$.
Hence:
:$\dfrac {BD} {DC} = \dfrac {\sqbrk {ABD} - \sqbrk {PBD} } {\sqbrk {ADC} - \sqbrk {PDC} } = \dfrac {\sqbrk {ABP} } {\sqbrk {APC} }$
